description.en: Understand WebSocket protocol, build real-time features with Python, and compare WebSockets to HTTP polling.
description.ta: WebSocket நெறிமுறையைப் புரிந்துகொள்ளுங்கள், Python மூலம் நிகழ்நேர அம்சங்களை உருவாக்குங்கள், மற்றும் HTTP polling-உடன் WebSockets-ஐ ஒப்பிடுங்கள்.

story_variants.en:
## The Walkie-Talkie

Vaathiyaar holds up a walkie-talkie and a postal letter. "HTTP is like postal mail — you send a request, wait for a reply. WebSockets are like walkie-talkies — once connected, both sides can talk at ANY time, instantly."

### HTTP vs WebSockets

| Feature | HTTP | WebSocket |
|---------|------|-----------|
| Connection | New per request | Persistent |
| Direction | Client → Server | Bidirectional |
| Overhead | Headers each time | Minimal after handshake |
| Use case | Page loads, APIs | Chat, live updates, games |
| Protocol | `http://` / `https://` | `ws://` / `wss://` |

### How WebSockets Work
1. Client sends HTTP upgrade request
2. Server agrees → connection upgrades to WebSocket
3. Both sides can send messages freely
4. Connection stays open until closed

### When to Use WebSockets
- **Chat applications** — instant message delivery
- **Live dashboards** — real-time data updates
- **Collaborative editing** — Google Docs style
- **Gaming** — multiplayer state sync
- **Notifications** — push alerts

### When NOT to Use WebSockets
- Simple CRUD APIs (use REST)
- Infrequent updates (use polling or SSE)
- One-way server updates (use Server-Sent Events)

> **Key Concept:** WebSockets maintain a persistent, bidirectional connection. This eliminates the overhead of repeated HTTP requests, making them ideal for real-time features. But they use more server resources per connection.

import asyncio
import websockets

async def chat_client():
    async with websockets.connect('ws://localhost:8000/ws/chat/bot') as ws:
        await ws.send('Hello from Python!')
        response = await ws.recv()
        print(f'Received: {response}')

asyncio.run(chat_client())

under_the_hood.summary: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request asking to upgrade; after the server answers 101 Switching Protocols, the same TCP connection stays open and both sides send small framed messages whenever they like.

steps.title: It begins as HTTP
steps.body: new WebSocket('wss://chat.example.com/ws') sends an ordinary GET with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key. Starting as HTTP lets WebSockets pass through the same ports (80 and 443), proxies and load balancers as normal web traffic.

steps.title: The server proves it understood
steps.body: The server appends the fixed GUID 258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11 to the key, takes the SHA-1 and base64-encodes it. For the key above that gives s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=, sent back as Sec-WebSocket-Accept with status 101 Switching Protocols. From now on the connection no longer carries HTTP.

steps.title: Messages travel as frames
steps.body: Each message is a frame with a small header: an opcode (1 text, 2 binary, 8 close, 9 ping, 10 pong), the payload length and the data. A short chat message costs only a few bytes of framing instead of a full set of HTTP headers. Frames from the browser are masked with a 4-byte key, as the protocol requires.

steps.title: Either side can speak first
steps.body: Because the connection stays open, the server can push a message the moment something happens, such as a new chat line or a price change, with no polling. Ping and pong frames keep idle connections alive and detect dead ones.

steps.title: The server holds many connections
steps.body: A Python server built with asyncio (for example the websockets library or FastAPI's WebSocket support) keeps each open connection as a coroutine waiting on await websocket.recv(). Thousands can wait at once on one event loop. Broadcasting to a chat room is a loop that awaits send() on every connection in the room's set.

under_the_hood.takeaway: WebSockets reuse HTTP only to get started. After the 101 upgrade, it is one long-lived connection carrying tiny frames in both directions.
